Hill Numbers

Source: R/alpha_div.r
hill.Rd

The effective number of species of order \(q\): how many equally abundant features would give the same diversity.

Usage

hill(counts, q = 2, margin = 1L, cpus = n_cpus())

Arguments

counts

A numeric matrix of count data (samples \(\times\) features). Typically contains absolute abundances (integer counts), though proportions are also accepted.

q

The order of a Hill number, or of Rényi's or Tsallis's entropy: a single number of at least 0, where Inf is allowed. Only used by hill(), renyi() and tsallis(). Default: 2, as scikit-bio (which calls it order).

margin

The margin containing samples. 1 if samples are rows, 2 if samples are columns. Ignored when counts is a special object class (e.g. phyloseq). Default: 1

cpus

How many parallel processing threads should be used. The default, n_cpus(), is the CPU cores this R process may use, within any limits set on it. Results are the same for any cpus.

Details

The Hill number of order \(q\) is defined as: $${}^qD = \left(\sum_{i = 1}^{n} P_i^q\right)^{1/(1-q)}$$

with its limits \({}^1D = e^H\) (\(H\): Shannon's entropy) and \({}^\infty D = 1 / \max(P_i)\).

Where:

  • \(n\) : The number of features.

  • \(P_i\) : Proportional abundance of the \(i\)-th feature.

The order sets how much weight abundant features get. The Hill numbers are a profile that unifies the common indices:

  • \(q = 0\): richness, observed().

  • \(q = 1\): the exponential of Shannon's entropy, exp(shannon()), which weighs every feature by its frequency (Jost 2006).

  • \(q = 2\): the inverse Simpson index, inv_simpson().

  • \(q = \infty\): the inverse Berger-Parker index, 1 / berger().

The default order, 2, is scikit-bio's, which makes hill() equal to inv_simpson(); give q for any other order. renyi() is log(hill()), and tsallis() is another function of it.

Observed Hill numbers grow with sequencing depth, most for small \(q\); compare samples at equal depth, for instance with alpha_div_rarefied().

Base R Equivalent:

x <- ex_counts[1,]
q <- 2
p <- x[x > 0] / sum(x)
sum(p ** q) ** (1 / (1 - q))

Same names in other packages

scikit-bio's hill() is the same (its order is q). vegan::renyi(x, scales, hill = TRUE) gives a profile of Hill numbers over several orders.

Input Types

The counts parameter is designed to accept a simple numeric matrix, but seamlessly supports objects from the following biological data packages:

  • phyloseq

  • rbiom

  • SummarizedExperiment

  • TreeSummarizedExperiment

For large datasets, standard matrix operations may be slow. See vignette('performance') for details on using optimized formats (e.g. sparse matrices) and parallel processing.

References

Hill, M. O. (1973). Diversity and evenness: a unifying notation and its consequences. Ecology, 54, 427-432. doi:10.2307/1934352

Jost, L. (2006). Entropy and diversity. Oikos, 113, 363-375. doi:10.1111/j.2006.0030-1299.14714.x

See also

alpha_div(), renyi(), tsallis(), vignette('adiv')

Other Diversity metrics: brillouin(), fisher(), inv_simpson(), renyi(), shannon(), simpson(), tsallis()

Examples

    hill(ex_counts)
#>   Saliva     Gums     Nose    Stool 
#> 2.029446 1.233425 2.783607 1.013125 
    
    # Richness, exp(Shannon), inverse Simpson
    sapply(c(0, 1, 2), function (q) hill(ex_counts, q = q))
#>        [,1]     [,2]     [,3]
#> Saliva    4 2.098450 2.029446
#> Gums      5 1.443173 1.233425
#> Nose      6 3.133746 2.783607
#> Stool     5 1.049432 1.013125
